Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

before putting the tools away i check that the hose is drained and hung on its hook and that the net is not resting in the water i write the date and anything unusual in a notebook on the bench this morning i’ll note that the pump intake had a maple seed and that the water level was still at the pencil mark i also note whether i topped up or trimmed anything because that helps me tell routine evaporation from a leak later on then i walk once around the pond and make sure the stones are stable the socket cover is closed and the spillway is running evenly that is the whole check it takes about twenty minutes when nothing needs extra attention", "output": "I’m going to walk through how I check and care for the small garden pond behind the shed. It is roughly eight feet long and five feet across, and the deepest part is eighteen inches. I measured it last spring with a marked bamboo cane. The pond has a flexible liner, a shallow shelf on the north side, and a small pump that sends water through a low stone spillway. I do this in the morning, before the sun reaches the water, because I can see the surface clearly and the fish are less active. I keep a bucket, a soft net, a hose, and a pair of gloves beside the bench, but I don’t leave the hose connected overnight.

First, I stand still for a minute and look before touching anything. I check whether the water is moving over the spillway and listen for the steady hum of the pump. If the water is quiet, I look at the pump outlet and the intake basket before assuming the pump has stopped. Last week, a maple seed had caught on the basket, and the pump was still running; it was just pushing less water. I remove leaves with the net and set them in a tub, not on the path, because wet leaves make the stones slippery. I also look for an oily film or a sharp, unusual smell. There is sometimes pollen on the surface in May, and that is different from an oily film. I don’t scoop out clear water just because it has a little dust on it.

Then I check the water level against a small pencil mark on the stone at the edge. A little drop over several warm days can be ordinary evaporation, but a quick drop needs a closer look. I check the liner edge and the ground around the pond for a wet patch. I top up slowly with tap water through the hose, but I use a spray nozzle so the water does not dig into the gravel. I usually add about one inch, not four inches in one go. If I have to add more, I do it in stages and let the water settle between them. I don’t add cold water directly over the fish, and I don’t refill while cleaning the pump because I want to see whether the level stays steady afterward.

1. Switch the pump off at the outdoor socket before lifting it.
2. Lift the pump by its handle, and not by the cable.
3. Open the intake cover and rinse the sponge in a bucket of pond water.
4. Check the impeller for grit and turn it gently with a finger.
5. Put the cover back and lower the pump onto its flat brick.

The bucket water looks dirty, but I pour it under the shrubs instead of back into the pond. I rinse the sponge once or twice until the larger bits are gone. I don’t scrub it until it looks new because the sponge holds helpful bacteria. My neighbor said, “The heron visits around dusk,” so I leave the pump cable looped high on the bank and keep the electrical connection dry. I don’t use household detergent or a wire brush on any part that goes back into the pond.

When I’m done with the pump, I turn it on and watch the spillway for a full minute. The flow should be even and should land on the flat stone rather than splash against the liner. If it splashes onto the liner, I move the stone a little instead of raising the pump. I check that the cable has slack and that it is not pinched under the brick. There is a small valve on the return tube, and I leave it at the pencil mark I made in April. I could turn it farther, but that would change the flow I’m trying to compare from one visit to the next. I wipe my hands before touching the outdoor socket and close its cover after switching on.

Next, I look at the fish without trying to catch them. Healthy fish usually move away when my shadow crosses the water. I watch for several minutes for one fish staying at the surface or leaning against the edge. I did see that once in July, when the afternoon was hot, and I moved a floating plant to make a little more shade. I don’t feed the fish during this morning check. If they finish their usual small feed slowly, I remove what remains rather than adding more. I avoid feeding when the water is very cold, and I never treat a cloudy patch with medicine just because it looks odd. If a fish seems unwell for more than a day, I write down what I saw and ask the local pond shop for advice.

There are two baskets of water lilies on the deep shelf and a clump of iris on the shallow shelf. I trim only leaves that are yellow or torn and keep the cut stems out of the water. I leave the healthy lily pads in place because they shade the pond in summer and give the fish cover. The iris can spread into the spillway, so I check the stones for a stem caught across the channel. I don’t pull hard if a root is stuck; I loosen the gravel around it first. In autumn, I remove fallen leaves more often, but I still leave a few small bits of plant matter in the baskets rather than stripping every surface clean.

Before putting the tools away, I check that the hose is drained and hung on its hook and that the net is not resting in the water. I write the date and anything unusual in a notebook on the bench. This morning, I’ll note that the pump intake had a maple seed and that the water level was still at the pencil mark. I also note whether I topped up or trimmed anything because that helps me tell routine evaporation from a leak later on. Then I walk once around the pond and make sure the stones are stable, the socket cover is closed, and the spillway is running evenly. That is the whole check. Keep the supplied language.", "input": "last october i spent an evening at the old tide mill in port ellis while the lantern room players recorded their radio drama the north window. i had gone because my neighbor mara vell was playing the station keeper and she had said i could sit quietly near the sound table. the mill stands beside the harbor road, with a green door that sticks when the weather is damp. that night the rain kept tapping the windows, and the whole building smelled of wet rope and coffee. i expected to watch a few takes and go home, but the recording lasted until nearly midnight.
new paragraph
there were six people in the room, though only three voices were on the episode. producer cal rusk sat beside an old mixing desk with masking tape on the faders. jo denby was the engineer, and she had brought a small metal case full of cables, batteries, and labeled adapters. mara wore her own wool coat over a blue costume blouse because the room was cold. i remember the sleeve kept brushing the microphone stand, so jo put a folded towel over the metal clip. it made a soft thump whenever mara turned toward the script. nobody treated the mistake as a crisis. they shifted the stand and tried the line again.
new paragraph
cal explained that the drama was set in 1948, after a storm had cut off a lighthouse from the mainland. the station keeper hears a knock at the door but cannot tell whether it comes from a person or from something loose on the roof. mara's character has to decide whether to open the door before the tide rises. the script had several pages of stage directions about wind, a kettle, and a clock that stopped at 11:17. cal said the clock sound was important because it gave listeners one fixed detail in a story where nobody knew what time it was. that seemed like a small idea, but the actors kept coming back to it.
new paragraph
section one, the first sound test. jo asked me to stand by the corridor door and close it slowly while she recorded from inside. on the first attempt, the latch clicked too sharply. we tried again with a strip of felt taped around the frame, and that made the door sound heavier, almost like it belonged in a stone building. cal listened through headphones and said, that's the one, leave the felt there. then he asked for three versions of the harbor wind. jo spun a paper tube near the microphone, mara rubbed a rough glove across a board, and i held a sheet of baking paper by the radiator. the baking paper sounded like rain, so they kept the glove and paper tube instead.
new paragraph
mara's first long scene began with the keeper saying, i know you are out there, but i don't know which one of us is afraid. she read it too quickly the first time. cal asked her to pause after out there, not because the character had solved anything, but because she was listening for an answer. mara nodded and said, i was pushing the sentence, i'll let the silence carry that part. on the next take, the pause felt so long that i looked at the clock, then remembered the clock in the script was supposed to be stopped. the actors did not laugh, but jo smiled behind the glass. that take went into the evening's working reel.
new paragraph
around ten, the power in the hallway flickered, and the red recording light went dark for a few seconds. jo checked the plugs, cal checked the recorder, and mara stayed at the microphone with one hand resting on the script. the file had saved up to the last completed line, but they listened to it before deciding where to begin again. cal said, let's restart at the kettle cue, no, the line just before it, so the breath matches. jo marked the place with a pencil in the margin. they repeated the passage twice, and the second version had a tiny chair creak that nobody had heard during the take. they kept it because it sounded like the keeper shifting her weight.
new paragraph
section two, what i noticed from the corridor. first, the actors used ordinary voices rather than whispering every frightening line. second, the quiet sounds took more attention than the loud ones: a spoon touching a cup, paper folded once, and mara's thumb sliding along the edge of a page. third, the people in the room waited through each take without talking, even when a sound had to be made several times. during a break, jo told me that silence on radio is never truly empty, because the listener still hears the room they are sitting in. i thought about that later on the bus home, where the heater clicked every few minutes and the windows shook at the corners.
new paragraph
before the final scene, mara asked whether the keeper should say the visitor's name. cal answered, she doesn't know it yet, so let the question stay unanswered. they recorded two endings, one with the door opening and one with the latch lifting but no footsteps coming inside. i was not told which ending they planned to use. at the end of the session, cal wrapped the reels in brown paper, and jo wrote the date and scene numbers on a card. mara thanked me for holding the corridor door, and i said the felt had done most of the work. walking back along the harbor road, i could still hear the paper tube making wind. the mill's green door stuck behind me, and for a second the ordinary latch sounded like the one from the play.", "output": "Last October I spent an evening at the old Tide Mill in Port Ellis while the Lantern Room Players recorded their radio drama, The North Window. I had gone because my neighbor Mara Vell was playing the station keeper, and she had said I could sit quietly near the sound table. The mill stands beside the harbor road, with a green door that sticks when the weather is damp. That night the rain kept tapping the windows, and the whole building smelled of wet rope and coffee. I expected to watch a few takes and go home, but the recording lasted until nearly midnight.

There were six people in the room, though only three voices were on the episode. Producer Cal Rusk sat beside an old mixing desk with masking tape on the faders. Jo Denby was the engineer, and she had brought a small metal case full of cables, batteries, and labeled adapters. Mara wore her own wool coat over a blue costume blouse because the room was cold. I remember the sleeve kept brushing the microphone stand, so Jo put a folded towel over the metal clip. It made a soft thump whenever Mara turned toward the script. Nobody treated the mistake as a crisis. They shifted the stand and tried the line again.

Cal explained that the drama was set in 1948, after a storm had cut off a lighthouse from the mainland. The station keeper hears a knock at the door but cannot tell whether it comes from a person or from something loose on the roof. Mara's character has to decide whether to open the door before the tide rises. The script had several pages of stage directions about wind, a kettle, and a clock that stopped at 11:17. Cal said the clock sound was important because it gave listeners one fixed detail in a story where nobody knew what time it was. That seemed like a small idea, but the actors kept coming back to it.

Section 1: The first sound test. Jo asked me to stand by the corridor door and close it slowly while she recorded from inside. On the first attempt, the latch clicked too sharply. We tried again with a strip of felt taped around the frame, and that made the door sound heavier, almost like it belonged in a stone building. Cal listened through headphones and said, “That's the one. Leave the felt there.” Then he asked for three versions of the harbor wind. Jo spun a paper tube near the microphone, Mara rubbed a rough glove across a board, and I held a sheet of baking paper by the radiator. The baking paper sounded like rain, so they kept the glove and paper tube instead.

Mara's first long scene began with the keeper saying, “I know you are out there, but I don't know which one of us is afraid.” She read it too quickly the first time. Cal asked her to pause after “out there,” not because the character had solved anything, but because she was listening for an answer. Mara nodded and said, “I was pushing the sentence. I'll let the silence carry that part.” On the next take, the pause felt so long that I looked at the clock, then remembered the clock in the script was supposed to be stopped. The actors did not laugh, but Jo smiled behind the glass. That take went into the evening's working reel.

Around ten, the power in the hallway flickered, and the red recording light went dark for a few seconds. Jo checked the plugs, Cal checked the recorder, and Mara stayed at the microphone with one hand resting on the script. The file had saved up to the last completed line, but they listened to it before deciding where to begin again. Cal said, “Let's restart at the kettle cue—no, the line just before it, so the breath matches.” Jo marked the place with a pencil in the margin. They repeated the passage twice, and the second version had a tiny chair creak that nobody had heard during the take. They kept it because it sounded like the keeper shifting her weight.

Section 2: What I noticed from the corridor. First, the actors used ordinary voices rather than whispering every frightening line. Second, the quiet sounds took more attention than the loud ones: a spoon touching a cup, paper folded once, and Mara's thumb sliding along the edge of a page. Third, the people in the room waited through each take without talking, even when a sound had to be made several times. During a break, Jo told me that silence on radio is never truly empty, because the listener still hears the room they are sitting in. I thought about that later on the bus home, where the heater clicked every few minutes and the windows shook at the corners.

Before the final scene, Mara asked whether the keeper should say the visitor's name. Cal answered, “She doesn't know it yet, so let the question stay unanswered.” They recorded two endings, one with the door opening and one with the latch lifting but no footsteps coming inside. I was not told which ending they planned to use. At the end of the session, Cal wrapped the reels in brown paper, and Jo wrote the date and scene numbers on a card. Mara thanked me for holding the corridor door, and I said the felt had done most of the work. Walking back along the harbor road, I could still hear the paper tube making wind. The mill's green door stuck behind me, and for a second the ordinary latch sounded like the one from the play."}]
